narrative.text: A glossary defining terms used in the manual, such as vaccination failure, data mining, signal, surveillance and vaccine. It explains, for example, that vaccine failure can be primary or secondary and can also result from faulty administration.
A list of the French acronyms used in the manual, covering vaccines, committees and conditions such as GBS and ITP.

Introduces the manual by describing immunization as a highly effective public health intervention and citing global coverage and deaths averted. It argues that as more vaccines are used, adverse events must be monitored and that causality assessment underpins risk assessment and decisions on AEFI.

Defines an adverse event following immunization and the cause-specific categories: vaccine product-related, vaccine quality defect-related, immunization error-related, immunization anxiety-related and coincidental events.

Explains the concept of causality and why it is hard to tell whether a vaccine actually caused an adverse event, given that vaccination often coincides with the onset of other illnesses. It stresses weighing all possible explanations before attributing an event to the vaccine or another cause.

Describes causality assessment as a systematic review of case data to judge how likely a link to the vaccine is, and lists what its quality depends on, such as reporting systems, medical and laboratory services and the review process. It cites the withdrawal of a rotavirus vaccine linked to intussusception as an example of its importance.
A heading introducing the levels at which AEFI causality assessment should be carried out.

Outlines the three levels of causality assessment (population, individual case and signal investigation) and, for the population level, lists criteria such as temporal relationship, strength and consistency of association and biological plausibility. Footnotes point to Institute of Medicine and WHO vaccine reaction-rate resources.

Explains that a single case report rarely proves causation but individual assessment helps detect new reactions and preventable errors, and that identifying coincidental events wrongly blamed on vaccines protects public confidence. It notes that rechallenge information, as in a case of recurrent Guillain-Barré syndrome after tetanus toxoid, can be informative.
States that signal investigation should consider all individual AEFI reports together with surveillance data, cluster investigations and non-clinical data.
Sets out which AEFI cases should be prioritised for causality assessment, notably serious events, events above expected rates, signals and others of concern to parents or communities.
Lists three prerequisites for causality assessment: a completed investigation, all case data available, and a valid diagnosis for the event.

Recommends that causality assessment be done by a multidisciplinary expert committee where possible, using available staff otherwise, and notes that WHO country and regional offices can provide technical support, giving WHO contact details.
Introduces the revised four-step process for assessing causality of an individual AEFI case, with separate assessment for each suspected vaccine when several are given.

Describes the four steps of the assessment (eligibility, checklist, algorithm and classification) and explains the eligibility step, which requires a valid diagnosis that meets a case definition such as those of the Brighton Collaboration. It refers to the assessment form in Annex 1 and ends with the template for framing the causality question.

Presents the checklist (Table 1) that guides reviewers in gathering evidence, organised by questions on other causes, known causal links with the vaccine or immunization, timing and evidence against causality. It notes that a comments column should be used and that the examples are not exhaustive.

Explains the first checklist question on whether clinical or laboratory evidence supports another cause, with examples such as an HPV vaccine death later attributed to a tumour and an encephalitis-like outbreak traced to Cassia occidentalis seeds.

Covers the checklist questions on known causal associations with the vaccine product, quality defects, immunization errors and immunization anxiety. Examples include vaccine-associated paralytic polio after oral polio vaccine, ITP after MMR vaccine and aseptic meningitis after the Urabe mumps strain. It also describes errors in handling, prescribing and administration and fainting linked to anxiety in adolescents.

Explains the checklist question on whether the event occurred within the time window of increased risk, using vaccine-associated paralytic polio (4 to 40 days after oral polio vaccine) as the example.
Covers the checklist question on strong evidence against a causal link, citing the reviews that found no evidence that MMR vaccine causes autism.

Describes additional factors that help classify an AEFI, such as background incidence rates, whether the event could reflect another condition and whether a similar event occurred after a previous dose. Examples include deaths among elderly people during an influenza campaign in Israel and a metabolic disorder found in twins after polio vaccination. It also discusses cases where the absence of standard criteria complicates interpretation, such as aseptic meningitis.

Explains how the algorithm (Figure 3) is applied after the checklist to guide reviewers toward a consistent, likely, indeterminate or unclassifiable result, while stressing it does not replace expert judgement. It adds that unclassifiable cases need further data.
Describes the final classification step, based on CIOMS/WHO vaccine pharmacovigilance definitions, and how the categories of consistent, indeterminate and inconsistent causal association are defined.
Lists the classification categories for cases with adequate information: consistent causal association (A1–A4), indeterminate (B1, B2) and inconsistent or coincidental (C).

States that cases lacking adequate information are unclassifiable and should be kept in a database for later review and signal analysis, followed by the template for summarising the classification reasoning.

Explains that causality assessment depends on the information available and the reviewers' skills, that conclusions may conflict and need expert resolution, and that new knowledge about mechanisms can change interpretations.
A section heading on the underlying mechanisms for classifying adverse events.
A heading for the category of consistent causal association with immunization.

Describes how the immune response to vaccines can cause common mild reactions and, rarely, serious ones, and lists mechanisms behind vaccine product-related and quality defect-related reactions. These include immune-mediated reactions, replication of attenuated or insufficiently inactivated agents, contaminants and direct toxic effects.

Explains that immunization error-related reactions are preventable and lists types of error, including faulty storage and handling, wrong prescribing or contraindications missed, incorrect administration and injury during or after vaccination, such as head trauma during fainting.
Lists reactions that anxiety about immunization can cause, including vasovagal, hyperventilation-related and stress-related psychiatric reactions.
A heading for the indeterminate causality category.
Describes category B1, where timing is consistent but evidence is insufficient, and says such cases should be stored in a national database so that similar reports can later reveal a signal.
Describes category B2, where investigation produces conflicting evidence for and against a causal link with immunization.
Introduces the category of inconsistent causal association (coincidence), noting that events may reflect underlying conditions or external exposures unrelated to vaccination.
Lists examples of underlying or emerging conditions, such as congenital or acquired conditions and psychogenic phenomena, that can explain coincidental events.
Lists external exposures that can cause coincidental events, such as infections, other drugs, non-vaccine allergens, environmental toxins and injuries.
Stresses that causality assessment should lead to action, such as training, research or system changes, to prevent problems recurring.
States that national immunization programmes should adopt standardised AEFI protocols agreed by a national committee for cases with a consistent causal association.
Says that confirmed vaccine product-related reactions should be handled according to each country's protocols.

Sets out actions for reactions linked to vaccine quality defects, including reviewing lot distribution, reporting to the national regulator and manufacturer, and informing WHO or the Uppsala Monitoring Centre.
States that training and capacity building are key to preventing immunization error-related reactions.
Advises vaccinating in a calm, safe setting to prevent immunization anxiety-related reactions.
A heading for actions on cases with indeterminate causality.
Advises keeping B1 cases in a national database so that they may later serve as a signal of a new or changed causal link.

Advises that B2 cases with conflicting evidence be reclassified if more information emerges, with reviewers seeking further data and expert advice, including from WHO's Global Advisory Committee on Vaccine Safety.
Advises communicating a coincidental classification to patients, families, health workers and the public.

Concludes that AEFI causality assessment resembles a differential diagnosis and should not be made on inadequate information, and encourages users to check minimum criteria and adapt the revised process to many settings.
The heading of Annex 1, the causality assessment form.

The checklist page of the Annex 1 causality assessment form, with yes/no/unknown/not applicable boxes for each question on other causes, known links, timing and other factors, plus eligibility questions on the valid diagnosis.
The algorithm page of the Annex 1 form, instructing reviewers to work through each step and record comments.
The classification page of the Annex 1 form, with boxes to tick and space to summarise the reasoning for the classification.
The heading of Annex 2, which contains worked examples.

Presents a worked example from a French-language manual on assessing causality of adverse events following immunization: a five-month-old boy develops fever, focal seizures and altered consciousness days after a second dose of a meningococcal C conjugate vaccine. Investigations find herpes virus on CSF PCR and brain inflammation on MRI, and he recovers on antiviral treatment; the case is noted to meet the Brighton Collaboration encephalitis definition at level 2 certainty.
A heading only, for step 1 (eligibility criteria) of the first causality-assessment example.

The completed step 2 checklist for the meningococcal vaccine and seizures example, marking yes/no/unknown answers on other causes, known vaccine links, vaccination errors, immunization anxiety and timing. It records herpes-positive CSF as strong evidence of another cause and frames the question of whether the vaccine caused the meningoencephalitis.
A heading for step 3 (algorithm) of the first example, instructing the reader to review all steps and tick the boxes.
Step 4 of the first example, concluding that the meningoencephalitis is unlikely to be vaccine-related (coincidental) because a confirmed herpes infection explains it.

Introduces a second example in which a two-year-old boy in a polio-endemic country develops sudden flaccid paralysis of the left arm after receiving many oral polio vaccine doses. It describes the investigation, stool sampling that isolates Sabin type 1 and 2 polioviruses, and a follow-up examination showing persisting weakness and wasting of the arm.
A heading only, for step 1 (eligibility criteria) of the oral polio vaccine and acute flaccid paralysis example.

The completed step 2 checklist for the oral polio vaccine and acute flaccid paralysis example, noting that vaccine-associated paralytic polio is a known event and that Sabin strains were found in the stool. Most vaccine-error and anxiety items are left blank, and the question asked is whether the vaccine caused the paralysis.
A heading for step 3 (algorithm) of the second example, asking the reader to tick the appropriate boxes.

Notes on step 3 of the polio example, judging a vaccine cause probable given the known association and timing while recording that other causes of flaccid paralysis exist but information on them is inadequate.

Sets out a third example: an 18-month-old girl in South Asia who died ten days after receiving MMR vaccine, giving her birth and vaccination history, the illness preceding her death and clinical findings. It also reports the ministry's field investigation of the vaccine lot, cold chain and vaccine vial monitor, and notes that other children given the same vaccine that day had no similar events.
A heading for option 1 of the third example, assessing MMR vaccine and thrombocytopenia.

The completed step 2 checklist for the MMR and thrombocytopenia option, recording that dengue is suspected but unconfirmed and that measles vaccine can cause thrombocytopenia but not severely enough to be fatal. It frames the question of whether MMR caused the fatal thrombocytopenia.

Notes on step 3 of the MMR and thrombocytopenia option, citing the known measles vaccine link and timing alongside the absence of haemorrhage at autopsy and possible other viral infections such as dengue.

Step 4 for the thrombocytopenia option, classifying the causal link as indeterminate or unlikely because the cause of low platelets cannot be determined and the autopsy found no haemorrhage, so the vaccine did not contribute to the death.
A heading for option 2 of the third example, assessing MMR vaccine and sepsis.

The completed step 2 checklist for the MMR and sepsis option, noting suspected but untested dengue and leaving most vaccine-related items unmarked. It frames the question of whether MMR caused the fatal sepsis and cites a published case definition.
Notes on step 3 of the sepsis option, suggesting the sepsis may have complicated a respiratory infection and that other infections such as probable dengue and a pre-vaccination fever were present.

Step 4 of the sepsis option, classifying the vaccine link as indeterminate or unlikely since the sepsis could stem from a respiratory infection or another viral illness, while acknowledging the vaccine may have worsened an existing infection. The block ends with the back-cover text and WHO contact details for vaccine safety.

Front matter of the French edition of WHO's user manual for the revised classification of causality assessment for adverse events following immunization (AEFI), with title pages, cataloguing data and ISBN, and the 2016 copyright and disclaimer text. It credits the subgroup of the Global Advisory Committee on Vaccine Safety that developed the protocol and notes the concepts draw on the CIOMS/WHO vaccine pharmacovigilance terminology. It also states the manual's purpose and gives the table of contents through the four assessment steps.
